name: Weapon focus effect
statement: A witness who sees a weapon is said to remember the person holding it less well, and the claim holds up better for descriptions than for lineup identification.
meaning: The claim is about attention and memory, not fear. A weapon in the scene is held to draw looking time away from the perpetrator, so less of the perpetrator gets encoded. Three outcomes are used to test this and they behave differently. The first is memory for the weapon itself, which is usually good. The second is feature or description accuracy: what a witness can say afterwards about the perpetrator's face, build, hair and clothing. The third is identification accuracy: whether the witness picks the right person out of a lineup, and whether they pick an innocent person out of a lineup the perpetrator is absent from. Almost every popular account of weapon focus is describing the third measure, and the third measure is where the evidence is weakest. The cross-race effect entry covers the other main estimator variable in eyewitness identification, and the two are usually tested in the same archival datasets.

origin.who: Elizabeth F. Loftus, Geoffrey R. Loftus and Jane Messo
origin.note: 'Some facts about "weapon focus"' put subject-witnesses in front of slides of a fast-food restaurant. Half saw a customer point a gun at the cashier, half saw him hand over a cheque. The paper's own abstract calls the result 'the first direct empirical support for weapon focus', so the phenomenon was already named and argued about before this paper measured it.

evidence: Loftus, Loftus and Messo ran two experiments on University of Washington students, 36 in the first and 80 in the second. Experiment 1 recorded eye movements. Subjects made an average of 3.72 fixations on the gun against 2.44 on the cheque, t(34) = 2.63, p < .01, and those fixations lasted 242.0 milliseconds against 200.3, t(34) = 2.24, p < .025. Its memory results were weaker than its reputation. On the 20-item questionnaire the gun group scored 45.8% against 50.3%, t(34) = 1.37, with a one-tailed p between .05 and .10. On the seven questions about the robber the split was 45.5% against 51.1%, t(34) = 1.03, p > .10. Two of 18 gun subjects picked the right man from a 12-photo lineup, or 11.1%, against seven of 18 controls, or 38.9%, and the authors call that difference marginally significant, chi-square 3.71 with p between .05 and .06. Experiment 2 dropped the eye tracking, ran 40 subjects per condition and found the effect. Gun subjects answered 56% of the seven questions correctly against 67%, t(78) = 2.04, p < .05, and identified the robber 15% of the time against 35%, chi-square 4.27, p < .05. Steblay's meta-analysis pooled 19 tests. Its abstract reports a small effect of 0.13 for lineup identification and a moderate one of 0.55 for feature accuracy, and that is the split the whole literature has argued over since. Fawcett, Russell, Peace and Christie's meta-analysis is the large one. Its abstract gives an overall effect of weapon presence of g = 0.53, moderated by retention interval, exposure duration and threat, and not moderated by whether the event happened in a laboratory, a simulation or the real world. Kocab and Sporer's meta-analysis, run on person identifications and descriptions separately, found no significant effect on correct identifications from target-present lineups, none on false identifications from target-absent lineups, and none on overall identification decisions. It found a significant medium effect on the accuracy of descriptions, and reports that unusualness behaved the same way, affecting descriptions but not identifications.

examples.tag: The knife on the shop counter
examples.text: A shop assistant is robbed, and afterwards can describe the blade in detail and the man holding it hardly at all. The claim is about where her looking time went, not about how frightened she was.

examples.tag: The description that will not fill in
examples.text: Asked for the robber's hair, build and jacket, a witness to an armed raid gives less than a witness to the same scene without a weapon. Description accuracy is the measure on which the effect is steadiest.

The same witness views a lineup and either picks nobody or picks the wrong man. Whether the weapon made that outcome likelier is a separate claim from whether it thinned her description, and the two are usually told as one.

replication.headline: Three meta-analyses report an effect on descriptions and split over identification, and five preregistered experiments with 1,316 participants produced one marginal result and nothing else.
replication.detail: West, Mulligan and Bornstein set out to find moderators of the effect and could not produce the effect. They ran five preregistered experiments, recruiting 1,357 participants and analysing 1,316, across samples of 100 to 800. Materials came from studies that had previously shown the effect. Modality varied between videos and slides, weapon type between knife and gun, perpetrator gender, audio, and student against non-student samples. Four experiments produced no reliable effect on description or on identification. Experiment 4a, on 100 undergraduates, produced a marginal one on lineup identification, b = -1.04, z = -1.96, p = 0.0504, OR = 0.352, which is the half in the paper's title, and its Bayes factor of 0.678 left that result ambiguous. Experiment 3 and Experiment 4b produced reliable effects the other way, with better memory for armed perpetrators. Random-effects meta-analysis across all five gave Hedges' g = -0.138, 95% CI [-0.349, 0.073], p = 0.201, for target description, and an odds ratio of 0.841, 95% CI [0.541, 1.307], p = 0.440, for lineup identification. Their manipulation worked: threat ratings differed by an average d = 0.774 without the memory effect following. Körner, Faul and Nuthmann tested the attention account directly with eye-tracking, using stimuli built from a United States study that had reported large memory effects. Weapon presence did not reduce recall of the perpetrator's appearance in any of three experiments. Their Bayes factors favoured absence: BF01 = 4.0 with 68 participants viewing videos, 5.9 with 56 viewing slide shows, and 19.0 with 266 online. In Experiment 2 the gun did attract more gaze than the phone, and it did not cost viewing time on the perpetrator, which is the step the attention-shift account needs. The same group's 2024 study cuts the other way. Its eye-tracking experiment on 162 participants found no memory effect, with 77.71% correct in the knife condition against 76.71% for a water bottle. Its online experiment on 228 participants did find one where the video carried sound, knife against water bottle t = 2.01, p = .024 one-tailed, d = 0.46, and found nothing where the sound was removed. A plunger, unusual but not threatening, produced a larger effect than the knife under the same conditions, d = 0.54.

study.cite: West, J. T., Mulligan, N. W., & Bornstein, B. H. (2026). Four (and a half) preregistered failures to replicate the weapon focus effect in online samples. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 32(1), 48-64.

replicated.weighting: random-effects across five experiments, target description

limits: The effect thins out wherever real crimes are involved. Valentine, Pickering and Darling analysed 640 identification attempts across 314 lineups run by the Metropolitan Police in London. Their abstract reports no independent, statistically reliable effect of weapon focus, and the same null for cross-race identification and for delay. Erickson and colleagues, writing on facial composites, put it that surveys of real cases show a weaker effect of weapon presence than of other factors such as perpetrator race and duration of encoding. Mansour, Hamilton and Gibson list Tollestrup and colleagues, Valentine and colleagues, and Yuille and Tollestrup as field analyses in which the effect was absent. Behrman and Davey's 271 police cases produced no reliable difference in lineup identification between weapon and no-weapon crimes, as Hatfield's review describes them. Tollestrup and colleagues are the archival exception, and their counts are small. Hatfield reports 44% of identification attempts producing a positive identification in weapon crimes, which is 21 attempts, against 71% without a weapon, which is seven. He reports the confound in the same breath. Police ran lineups in 51% of weapon offences and 23% of weaponless ones, so the two rates come from differently selected witnesses. Fawcett's abstract says the opposite about setting, reporting that laboratory, simulation and real-world events did not differ. Whether the archival record contains the effect is therefore an open disagreement between a meta-analysis and the individual studies it pooled, and this entry could not read the meta-analysis to see how it was resolved. Two of the three meta-analyses are paywalled. Steblay's article and Kocab and Sporer's chapter sit behind Springer, which serves their abstracts and not their text. Fawcett's is not a paywall case. Taylor & Francis answers with a bot challenge, and no repository copy was found through Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar, so the next reader may get further than this one did. Fawcett's separate estimate for feature accuracy could not be obtained from any of those sources. The identification figure, g = 0.22 for laboratory studies, is quoted from Carlson and colleagues' description of it, read in Semantic Scholar's citation-context index rather than in the article, and it is kept out of the structured fields for that reason. Archival counts from Tollestrup and colleagues and from Behrman and Davey are quoted here from Hatfield's undergraduate literature review, the only fetchable source located for them. Searches of Crossref and OpenAlex on 21 September 2026, and of the open web, located no multi-laboratory preregistered replication of the effect, and West and colleagues close their paper by calling for one. Their own five experiments were all online, and they allow that the effect may be real and dependent on methodological factors such as study modality.
misreadings: Three outcomes get treated as one. Steblay's pooled 0.13 for lineup identification and 0.55 for feature accuracy are not two estimates of the same thing, and Kocab and Sporer found the identification effects absent while the description effect held. A witness who cannot describe a robber well is a different problem from a witness who picks the wrong man, and only the second convicts anybody. The famous eye-tracking result is smaller than its reputation. Loftus, Loftus and Messo's Experiment 1 is the one everyone cites for the gaze data, and in that experiment neither memory questionnaire reached significance and the lineup difference was marginal. The significant memory results belong to Experiment 2, which recorded no eye movements. Threat is assumed to be the mechanism and the direct tests point elsewhere. Pickel crossed threat against unusualness in two experiments and found description accuracy affected by unusualness and not by threat, with identification accuracy not differing by condition at all. Mansour and colleagues note that a gun in a context where it belongs, such as a gun range, produces no effect. Fawcett's meta-analysis found weapons produced numerically but not reliably greater impairment than other unusual objects, as Carlson and colleagues describe it, and Körner and colleagues in 2024 found a plunger outperforming a knife on the same measure. Legal recognition runs ahead of the field evidence rather than with it. New Jersey's model criminal jury charge on identification, revised in May 2020, instructs jurors to consider whether the witness saw a weapon, citing State v. Henderson at 262-63. Seale-Carlisle and colleagues surveyed 76 eyewitness experts between December 2020 and June 2021, and 80% agreed that seeing a weapon can later affect identification performance. Fawcett, Peace and Greve wrote in 2016 that testimony on weapon focus is rarely admissible in court and argued it was robust enough to guide practice. West and colleagues, a decade later, say their results call that consensus into question. Every part of that recognition tracks the laboratory literature on identification, which is the part of the literature that has failed to replicate. The failure is not total. West and colleagues' own informal search of work published after 2020 turned up five papers and 16 tests, of which two were significant weapon focus effects, 13 were null and one ran the other way. The largest recent positive is Dodson and colleagues' study of 2,609 participants, which West and colleagues re-analysed and could reproduce only as a marginal effect in one condition.

sources.text: Loftus, E. F., Loftus, G. R., & Messo, J. (1987). Some facts about "weapon focus". Law and Human Behavior, 11(1), 55-62. Scanned reprint read in full on Geoffrey Loftus's University of Washington faculty page, with the text recovered by optical character recognition; the publisher's copy at Springer is paywalled. Source for the fixation counts and durations and for both experiments' memory results.

Steblay, N. M. (1992). A meta-analytic review of the weapon focus effect. Law and Human Behavior, 16(4), 413-424. Paywalled at Springer, which serves the article's landing page and abstract but not its text. The 19 tests, the 0.13 for lineup identification and the 0.55 for feature accuracy were read in that abstract on 21 September 2026.

Fawcett, J. M., Russell, E. J., Peace, K. A., & Christie, J. (2013). Of guns and geese: A meta-analytic review of the 'weapon focus' literature. Psychology, Crime & Law, 19(1), 35-66. Not read, and not because of a paywall: Taylor & Francis returns a bot challenge, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar record no repository copy. The overall g = 0.53 and the moderators come from the publisher abstract, read at OpenAlex and again at the colab.ws index.

Kocab, K., & Sporer, S. L. (2016). The weapon focus effect for person identifications and descriptions: A meta-analysis. In Advances in Psychology and Law (pp. 71-117). Springer. Paywalled; the abstract was read on the chapter's Springer page. Source for the null results on identification and the medium effect on descriptions. That abstract lists publication bias among the topics discussed without stating a finding, so the claim that this meta-analysis alone detected publication bias is taken from West and colleagues.

West, J. T., Mulligan, N. W., & Bornstein, B. H. (2026). Four (and a half) preregistered failures to replicate the weapon focus effect in online samples. Psychology, Public Policy, and Law, 32(1), 48-64. Full text read at PubMed Central, where the copy is the author manuscript posted on 21 July 2025 before final editing. Crossref gives the version of record as the February 2026 issue; the publisher's own site returns a bot challenge.

Körner, H. M., Faul, F., & Nuthmann, A. (2023). Revisiting the role of attention in the 'weapon focus effect': Do weapons draw gaze away from the perpetrator under naturalistic viewing conditions? Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 85(6), 1868-1887. Published version read in full as the open-access Springer PDF.

Körner, H. M., Faul, F., & Nuthmann, A. (2024). Is a knife the same as a plunger? Comparing the attentional effects of weapons and non-threatening unusual objects in dynamic scenes. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 9(1). Full text read as the JATS XML served by Europe PMC. Source for the null in the eye-tracking experiment and for the effect that appeared online with sound and vanished without it.

Mansour, J. K., Hamilton, C. M., & Gibson, M. T. (2019). Understanding the weapon focus effect: The role of threat, unusualness, exposure duration, and scene complexity. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 33(6), 991-1007. Accepted manuscript read in full at Queen Margaret University's repository.

Pickel, K. L. (1998). Unusualness and threat as possible causes of 'weapon focus'. Memory, 6(3), 277-295. Abstract read at colab.ws, which reproduces the publisher's; the source for description accuracy being affected by unusualness and not by threat, and for identification accuracy not differing by condition.

Valentine, T., Pickering, A., & Darling, S. (2003). Characteristics of eyewitness identification that predict the outcome of real lineups. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 17(8), 969-993. Abstract read at colab.ws on 21 September 2026; the source for the field null across 640 identification attempts in 314 real lineups. Wiley returns a bot challenge, and the accepted manuscript deposited at Queen Margaret University requires authentication.

Fawcett, J. M., Peace, K. A., & Greve, A. (2016). Looking down the barrel of a gun: What do we know about the weapon focus effect? Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 5(3), 257-263. Not read. The DOI resolves to a publisher site that answers with a bot challenge, as does the ScienceDirect copy, and Unpaywall records the article as open access, so this is not a paywall. The abstract was read through Semantic Scholar's interface and is the source for the claim that such testimony is rarely admissible.

Seale-Carlisle, T. M., Quigley-McBride, A., Teitcher, J., Crozier, W., Dodson, C. S., & Garrett, B. L. (2024). New insights on expert opinion about eyewitness memory research. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 20(5), 903-924. Full text read as the JATS XML served by Europe PMC; the source for 80% of 76 experts agreeing about weapon presence and for the survey running from December 2020 to June 2021.

New Jersey Courts. Model criminal jury charge, 'Identification: in-court and out-of-court identifications', revised 5/18/2020. Section (c) is headed Weapon Focus and its footnote cites State v. Henderson, 208 N.J. at 262-63. Read in full.

Erickson, W. B., Brown, C., Portch, E., Lampinen, J. M., Marsh, J. E., Fodarella, C., Petkovic, A., Coultas, C., Newby, A., Date, L., Hancock, P. J. B., & Frowd, C. D. (2022). The impact of weapons and unusual objects on the construction of facial composites. Psychology, Crime & Law, 30(3), 207-228. Open-access copy read in full at White Rose eprints; the source for real-case surveys showing a weaker weapon effect than perpetrator race or encoding duration.

Carlson, C. A., Pleasant, W. E., Weatherford, D. R., Carlson, M. A., & Bednarz, J. E. (2016). The weapon focus effect: Testing an extension of the unusualness hypothesis. Applied Psychology in Criminal Justice, 12(2). PDF read in full. Source for Fawcett's finding that weapons impaired memory numerically but not reliably more than other unusual objects, and for the 963 undergraduates in which only the handgun reduced identification accuracy.

Carlson, C. A., Young, D. F., Weatherford, D. R., Carlson, M. A., Bednarz, J. E., & Jones, A. R. (2016). The influence of perpetrator exposure time and weapon presence/timing on eyewitness confidence and accuracy. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 30(6), 898-910. Not read; Wiley and the Texas A&M San Antonio repository copy both answer with bot challenges. Its sentence giving Fawcett's laboratory identification estimate as g = 0.22 was read in Semantic Scholar's citation-context index.

Dodson, C. S., Seale-Carlisle, T. M., Garrett, B. L., Kafadar, K., & Yaffe, J. (2025). Persistence of the verbal overshadowing and weapon-focus effects on lineup identification performance. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 14(3), 416-427. Not read; the publisher answers with a bot challenge and the repository copy at Aberdeen was unreachable. Its sample of 2,609 and its conclusion are quoted here from West and colleagues, who cite it as 2024, the year of its advance publication.

Hatfield, T. Weapon focus effect: A literature review. Afficio Undergraduate Journal, Saint Mary's University. An undergraduate review, read in full, and the only fetchable source located for the archival counts attributed here to Tollestrup and colleagues and to Behrman and Davey.
